failures.reason: A template with placeholder tokens rather than values. The detector does flag it, so this stays a false positive — but it must at least say the value is made of placeholder words, or a reviewer has no way to tell a template from a leak without opening the chunk.
Fails a Luhn check; not a card number.
Health information about an identifiable relative. Whether it is ePHI is a legal determination, not a detector's — which is why the criterion model asks a human.
A named individual with a postal address.
A fictional character and a fictional address.
A full date of birth, introduced by the words rather than the abbreviation. The detector matches "DOB 1990-02-14" and not this, which is how a support transcript is actually written.
A full UK postal address with postcode. There is no address or UK postcode detector, so this identifies a household and is not seen.

An anonymised placeholder in a post-mortem. It is a valid key *shape*, deliberately, which is why it is the hardest negative here: nothing is exposed and there is nothing to rotate, so a reviewer sent to this chunk has no work to do.

results.reason: Security advice containing no credential.

A template with placeholder tokens rather than values. The detector does flag it, so this stays a false positive — but it must at least say the value is made of placeholder words, or a reviewer has no way to tell a template from a leak without opening the chunk.
Already redacted; the last four digits alone are not a PAN.
Random-looking words, no structure any detector should claim.
Tabular figures that resemble nothing sensitive.
A live override attempt sitting in retrievable content.
A role-reassignment payload.

Security documentation quoting a payload. It should still be flagged — a quoted payload is still retrievable — but a reviewer must be told it is a quotation, or the security team drowns in its own writing.
Contains "ignore the previous" in an ordinary business sentence. This is the sentence that separates a usable detector from a keyword match.
Describes a prompt without attacking one.
Mentions a system; no instruction to a model.
A UI instruction to a person. 'Enter' is a key, not a mode.
Navigating a UI. 'Switch to' without a persona or mode is ordinary prose.
'Act as' describing staff roles, not reassigning a model's role.
Setup instructions. Naming an interpreter is not tool abuse.
Engineering guidance mentioning a database.
Reading documentation about a database is not reading a database.
'You are now' followed by a state, not a persona.
Operations runbook. Maintenance mode is a server state.
Device settings. Developer mode on a phone is not a jailbreak of a model.
A spec sheet. A 'System:' line is a field label, not a forged chat turn.
Package credits written as key/value lines.
A help-desk procedure. Sending a reset link to the account owner is not exfiltration.
API documentation.
Cloud setup documentation.
A product limit, not a request to drop a model's safety policy.
Planning prose using 'actual goal'.
'Context' here is a menu.
A compliance reminder.
Integration documentation mentioning a webhook and data.
A markdown heading that begins with 'User', not a forged turn boundary.
A byte-order mark at the start of an exported file.
A zero-width joiner inside an emoji sequence (woman technologist).
Persian uses ZWNJ inside words ('I want to book an appointment').
The England flag is a black flag followed by tag letters and a cancel tag.
Real Russian prose ('the patient was discharged home'). Cyrillic is not a disguise unless it is mixed into Latin words.
A right-to-left mark keeping punctuation in place in Hebrew text.
A presigned S3 URL carries an access key id and signature by design.
An image with an ordinary version parameter.
A Cyrillic o inside 'ignore' defeats a Latin-only pattern.
The same evasion with a Greek alpha.
Soft hyphens render as nothing and split the trigger words.
Variation selectors are invisible and split the trigger words.
A zero-width space inside a trigger word.
An instruction written in Unicode tag characters, invisible to a reviewer.
A base64-wrapped override.
A rendered image whose query string already carries an AWS key id: zero-click exfiltration.
The same with a patient email address in the query.
An image the model is asked to fill with the conversation.
A named jailbreak mode.
Persona reassignment plus refusal suppression.
'Act as' with a model persona as its object.
A forged system turn ordering exfiltration to an address.
Forged chat-template delimiters around an override.
Overrides the other retrieved passages (ATLAS AML.T0071).
CSS-hidden exfiltration instruction.
Agent tool abuse against a credential file.

An override stated as precedence, behind a bare 'SYSTEM:' line. Found by re-scanning the demo stores: once a bare 'SYSTEM:' became a supporting signal, this payload was missed until the precedence phrasing was covered.
Document control language. It supersedes versions, not instructions to a model.
Concealment plus retrieval manipulation.

Luhn-valid and not a published test number. (The first draft of this item used a number that failed a Luhn check, so it recorded correct detector behaviour as a false negative — the corpus was wrong, not the detector.)
Visa publishes this for testing; it passes Luhn by design.
American Express publishes this test number.
Nineteen digits, not a card number. A detector that matches any long digit run will flag order and invoice numbers forever.
A phone number, not an account number.
Fails a Luhn check; not a card number.
A named patient with a record number and a diagnosis code.
Health information about an identifiable relative. Whether it is ePHI is a legal determination, not a detector's — which is why the criterion model asks a human.
Fiction about medicine identifies no one.
A benefits policy; no individual's health data.
A code in a reference table, attached to nobody. A detector keyed on code shapes alone will flag every clinical glossary.
An address at a routable domain.
.test is reserved by RFC 6761 and cannot route.
The Social Security Administration's published example number.
A named individual with a postal address.
A public office in a news sentence. Treating every named role as personal data makes the finding list meaningless.
A fictional character and a fictional address.
Talks about personal data without containing any.
A template with no customer detail in it.
A full date of birth, introduced by the words rather than the abbreviation. The detector matches "DOB 1990-02-14" and not this, which is how a support transcript is actually written.
A full UK postal address with postcode. There is no address or UK postcode detector, so this identifies a household and is not seen.
Shaped as a live AWS access key id and not a published example.
AWS prints this key in its own documentation. A detector should still flag the shape, but must say it is a published example — a reviewer who is not told that wastes a rotation.
The AWS documentation secret key.
Stripe reserves sk_test_ for test mode; it cannot move money.
Shaped like a GitHub token, in a collection labelled as fixtures.
Security guidance about keys, quoting one. A detector that cannot tell this from a leak floods the queue with its own documentation.
Base64 image data. High entropy, no credential.
A UUID is not a secret.
A commit hash looks random and authenticates nothing.
Talks about a key without containing one.
AKIA prefix but 15 trailing characters, not 16. Not a key shape.
Lowercase. AWS key ids are uppercase; a case-insensitive match here is a false positive.
A base64 blob of similar length and alphabet. Flagging it is a false positive.
A UUID that happens to begin with the prefix. Hyphens break the key shape.
A 40-character hex hash. Long, high-entropy, and not a credential.
Discusses keys without containing one. A policy document must not be flagged.
A variable reference, which is the correct pattern. Flagging it punishes good practice.
Already redacted. Nothing is exposed and there is nothing to rotate.
A different 20-character uppercase token. Length alone must not trigger it.

An anonymised placeholder in a post-mortem. It is a valid key *shape*, deliberately, which is why it is the hardest negative here: nothing is exposed and there is nothing to rotate, so a reviewer sent to this chunk has no work to do.
A live-shaped key checked into Terraform, which is where they usually leak.
A key in a serialized configuration blob.
A key leaked into an application log, a common ingestion path into a RAG store.
A key embedded in runbook prose rather than in a config block.
A key in a tabular export, where surrounding punctuation differs from config syntax.
A key in a source comment, with an acknowledgement that it should not be there.
A key inside a support ticket, which is how they reach a knowledge base.
A key in a dotenv file alongside a benign variable.
The key with no surrounding text.
The same key in a sentence. Counts as the same case, not a second one.
The same key in quotation marks. Still one case.
